title: Small and real
hookLine: a practice you keep beats a perfect one you don't; the widow's two mites outweigh the rich gifts (Mark 12:41-44)
tomorrow: one went home and one stayed. which daughter-in-law was right?

lines: A BIG CHECK, A FOLDED TEN.
cards: Two gifts reach the school fundraiser in the same week: a big check from a company, and an envelope from a grandmother on a fixed income with a ten-dollar bill folded inside. On paper, one is far larger.
The Gospel of Mark has a scene about exactly that arithmetic. Jesus sits across from the temple treasury in Jerusalem, watching people drop in their offerings. Rich people come by and cast in much.
Then a poor widow comes, and she throws in two mites, two tiny coins. Jesus calls his disciples over. He wants them to see this one.

teach.b: "Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury." More? Two tiny coins?

Jesus explains: they gave out of their abundance, "but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living." Their gifts were big, and cost them nothing they'd miss. Hers was small, and it was real.
Here's the teaching Christians take from it.

teach.h: WEIGHED BY WHAT IT COST HER.
teach.b: In Jesus' accounting, a gift is weighed by what it costs the giver, not by the number on it. Now carry that to practice.

A grand plan written on a Sunday night is like the rich men's offerings: it looks large, and it hasn't cost anything yet. A practice you'll actually keep, five minutes, one Saturday, one call, is the widow's coins.
Notice what Jesus does not say.

teach.h: NOT SMALL FOR ITS OWN SAKE: REAL.
teach.b: He doesn't tell the rich to stop giving, and he doesn't praise small for being small. He praises real: the gift that's actually given, from what she actually had. So the question for any plan isn't, is it big enough?
It's, is it real? Will you put it in, this week, with what you've got?
Small and real beats large and imagined.

how: Christians read the widow's offering in Mark 12 as a teaching on giving from the heart, measured by what it costs the giver, not by its size.

o: a practice so easy it doesn't need any effort at all
a practice small enough to really keep, given wholeheartedly
a cheap version you do until you can afford the real one

games.q: the widow's mites: tap the pairs.
p: cast in much, out of their abundance
she cast in more than all of them
what it cost the giver, not the size

s: Jesus told the rich to stop giving their large offerings
he didn't. he praised the widow because her small gift was real and cost her everything.
Jesus said the widow gave more than all the others
they gave from abundance; she gave all she had, even all her living.
in this story, a small gift is better just because it's small
the point is real, not small: the gift actually given, from what she actually had.

games.q: your friend wants to start praying, but she's embarrassed: she can manage five minutes, and her aunt prays for an hour. what fits the widow's mites?
o: five minutes really given count; the widow's coins weren't measured against the rich.
wait until she can manage the hour; anything smaller doesn't count.
give up; if she can't match her aunt, it's better not to try.
games.why: Jesus didn't rank the widow below the rich for giving less; he said she gave more, because it was really given, from what she had.

practice: Take one plan you've made in this new stretch and shrink it until it fits your real week. Then do its smallest piece now: one line read, one glass of water for a plant, one slow minute of quiet.

wordCard.voice: Small and real: a practice you'll actually keep, like the widow's two mites, which Jesus said were more than all the rich men's gifts.

orig.note: Greek: lepta, small coins; the 'two mites' the widow gives in Mark 12:42.

carryVoice: Your line: small and real. Two coins, given whole, outweighed all the rest. That's day 1594.
